column1: ownership|When does assigning a Rust String move it rather than copy it?|String is not Copy: assignment transfers ownership and the old binding cannot be used. Clone explicitly duplicates its owned buffer; moving transfers the handle, not necessarily the heap allocation. Copy types duplicate implicitly.|move~ownership;Copy;clone|String assignment always deep-copies its buffer.|A String is assigned to another binding and the first is printed. Explain the compile failure and two fixes.|The first binding was moved. Borrow it when only reading, or clone when two independent owned strings are necessary; account for allocation cost.|rust-ownership|ownership

borrows|How do shared and mutable borrows prevent data races in safe Rust?|While references overlap, a value can have multiple shared references or one exclusive mutable reference. Non-lexical lifetimes can end a borrow after its last use. The restrictions preserve aliasing and mutation guarantees.|shared~immutable;exclusive~one mutable;last use~lifetime|A shared reference and a mutable reference may always overlap.|Can an immutable borrow be used again after a live mutable borrow mutates the same value?|Not while the borrows overlap. Reorder the last use, restrict scope, or restructure ownership; the compiler rejects the conflicting uses.|rust-borrow|mutable

lifetimes|What does a lifetime annotation establish, and can it extend an object's lifetime?|Annotations relate reference lifetimes for the borrow checker. They do not keep values alive. A returned borrow must refer to storage that outlives it; use owned data when no suitable borrowed owner survives.|relat~constraint;not~doesn't~cannot;outlive~owned|Adding a lifetime parameter keeps a local value alive.|A function returns a reference to a locally allocated String. Does adding lifetime a repair it?|No. The local String is dropped on return. Return String ownership, or borrow from input that survives; an annotation cannot create storage.|rust-lifetimes|outlive

strings|When should a Rust API accept String versus &str?|String owns a growable UTF-8 buffer; &str borrows a UTF-8 string slice. Accept &str for read-only access without ownership transfer, and String when ownership is required. Character indices are not arbitrary UTF-8 byte boundaries.|own~owned;borrow;UTF-8|String and &str are interchangeable allocation-free owned types.|Design a read-only label validator that accepts both String and string literals.|Accept &str, borrow a String with as_str or coercion, and avoid cloning. Validate Unicode carefully rather than indexing arbitrary bytes.|rust-strings|slice

box|When does Box<T> help with recursive Rust data structures?|Box provides unique ownership of a heap allocation and has a known pointer size. Indirection permits recursive types with finite compile-time size. Box does not add shared ownership or automatic thread synchronization.|heap;recursive~indirection;unique~ownership|Box makes a value shared across threads.|An enum directly contains another value of its own type. Why is a boxed recursive field useful?|The unboxed recursive layout has no finite size. A Box indirection gives the enum a finite pointer-sized recursive field and owns the child.|rust-box|recursive

rc-arc|How do Rc<T> and Arc<T> differ, and does Arc make T thread-safe?|Rc uses non-atomic reference counting for single-threaded sharing. Arc uses atomic reference counts for shared ownership across threads when T satisfies the required Send/Sync bounds. Mutable shared state still needs synchronization such as Mutex or atomics.|Rc;atomic;Send~Sync~synchron|Arc makes any contained type thread-safe.|Can Arc<RefCell<T>> replace Arc<Mutex<T>> in shared state used from multiple threads?|Not generally: RefCell is not Sync. Arc only synchronizes reference counts, not interior access. Use a suitable thread-safe lock or redesign ownership.|rust-arc,rust-send|atomic

send-sync|What do Rust Send and Sync mean?|Send permits ownership transfer between threads. Sync means a shared reference can be transferred safely, equivalently T is Sync when &T is Send. They are unsafe auto traits; do not add unsafe implementations without proving invariants.|ownership~transfer;shared~reference;auto~unsafe|Send means shared references are always thread-safe.|A type is Send but not Sync. May a worker own it exclusively while other threads retain shared references?|Moving ownership can be allowed, but sharing references still requires Sync. Design an ownership handoff instead of asserting a nonexistent shared-access guarantee.|rust-send|Send

result-option|When should an API return Option<T> versus Result<T,E>?|Option represents presence or absence through Some/None. Result distinguishes success from a failure carrying error information through Ok/Err. Neither requires exceptions; choose whether absence is an ordinary outcome or an error callers must diagnose.|Some~None;Ok~Err;error~absence|Option and Result represent the same failure information.|A missing optional profile field is normal, but a database connection failure needs diagnosis. Choose return types.|Use Option for a normal absent field and Result for the database failure; Result<Option<T>,E> can express both independently.|rust-errors|Result

question-operator|How does the Rust question-mark operator propagate errors?|On Result, ? returns the Ok value or returns early with an Err convertible to the enclosing function's error type. On Option it unwraps Some or returns None in an Option-returning context; it does not blindly convert Option into Result.|early~return;convert~From;Option~None|The question-mark operator panics on every error.|A Result-returning function calls an Option-returning lookup. How can it use question-mark?|Convert absence with ok_or or ok_or_else to a chosen error, then use ?. Do not assume the operator invents the missing error value.|rust-errors|operator

async|When does an async Rust function execute, and what drives progress?|Calling an async function produces a Future; work progresses when the future is polled, commonly by an executor. Awaiting can suspend the current future rather than blocking an operating-system thread. Creating a future does not automatically spawn a thread.|Future;poll~executor;suspend~thread|Every async function call spawns a separate operating-system thread.|An async function is called but its returned future is never awaited or spawned. Why are side effects missing?|The future was not driven to completion. Await it in another future or schedule it on an appropriate runtime, preserving cancellation and error handling.|rust-async|Future

async-borrow|Why can a spawned Rust future require owned or static data?|A task may outlive its caller, so many spawn APIs require a Send plus static future. Move owned data or an Arc into the task. Static does not mean data must live forever; borrowed stack data generally cannot satisfy that task boundary.|outlive~static;owned~Arc;Send|Static requires leaking every value for the lifetime of the process.|A background task borrows a local request String. How can the API avoid a dangling borrow?|Move ownership into the task or clone shared owned state, and respect the runtime's spawn bounds. A scoped or directly awaited future may allow different borrowing rules.|rust-async,rust-send|async

allocation|Do Rust moves always allocate, and what is stored by Vec<T>?|A move transfers ownership and does not inherently allocate. Vec owns a contiguous heap buffer and stores pointer, length, and capacity in its handle. Reallocation can occur when capacity grows; references cannot remain valid across an incompatible mutation.|move;heap~buffer;capacity~realloc|Every move performs a new heap allocation.|A tight loop clones a large Vec just to read it. Suggest a lower-allocation interface.|Pass a borrowed slice &[T] for reading, avoiding repeated deep clones. Reserve capacity for intentional growth and measure allocations rather than assuming moves copy the buffer.|rust-ownership|heap

refcell|How does RefCell<T> provide interior mutability, and when can it panic?|RefCell permits mutation through shared access while checking borrowing rules at runtime. borrow_mut conflicts with existing borrows and can panic; try_borrow variants return errors. RefCell is for single-threaded interior mutability, not concurrent shared mutation.|runtime;panic~try_borrow;single-thread~not Sync|RefCell removes borrowing restrictions entirely.|A callback re-enters code while a RefCell mutable borrow is still held. What failure can occur?|The second incompatible borrow can panic. Drop the guard before the callback, shorten scope, or use a fallible borrow and handle the error.|rust-refcell|runtime

mutex|How should Rust lock guards and poisoned Mutex errors be handled?|A Mutex guard releases the lock when dropped. Poisoning indicates a panic occurred while holding the lock, not proof that all data is corrupt. Decide whether invariants can be repaired before recovering; avoid holding locks through slow callbacks.|guard~drop;panic~poison;invariant~recover|A poisoned mutex can never be recovered.|A worker panics while updating shared state under a Mutex. Should the next caller blindly ignore PoisonError?|No. Inspect or restore the protected invariants, then recover with an explicit policy or fail the operation. Poisoning is advisory evidence of a possible invariant violation.|rust-mutex-api,rust-mutex|poison

async-lock|Why can blocking work or a long-held mutex hurt an async Rust service?|A blocking operation can occupy an executor thread and delay unrelated tasks. Move substantial blocking work to a runtime's blocking pool, keep critical sections short, and avoid holding unsuitable guards across await points. Use cancellation-aware timeouts and suitable async primitives when needed.|blocking;executor~thread;await~critical section|Adding async to a function makes blocking calls nonblocking.|An async handler performs a long synchronous filesystem operation while holding shared state. Redesign it.|Copy only needed state under a short lock, release it, run blocking work in a blocking pool, and reacquire state with version checks if a stale result would be unsafe.|rust-async,rust-mutex|await
